content: Prototheria is a taxonomic group, or taxon, to which the order Monotremata belongs. It is conventionally ranked as a subclass within the class Mammalia. Most of the animals within this group are extinct. The egg-laying monotremes are known from fossils dating back to the Cretaceous and Cenozoic periods. Today, they are represented by the platypus and several species of echidna. The terms Prototheria, Metatheria, and Eutheria translate to first beasts, changed beasts, and true beasts, respectively. These names refer to the three major mammalian groupings that have living representatives. Each of these groups can be defined as a clade that includes a living crown group (Monotremata, Marsupialia, and Placentalia, respectively) along with any fossil species more closely related to that crown group than to any other animals. The division of living mammals into monotremes, marsupials, and placentals was well established by the time Thomas Huxley introduced the terms Metatheria and Eutheria in 1880 to classify the latter two groups. Initially treated as subclasses, Metatheria and Eutheria are now conventionally grouped as infraclasses within the subclass Theria. More recent proposals have further demoted their taxonomic rank to cohorts or even magnorders, as cladistic analyses of relationships between living and fossil mammals have suggested that Theria itself should be reduced in rank. Prototheria, on the other hand, was generally recognized as a subclass until relatively recently. This classification was based on a hypothesis that defined the group by two supposed synapomorphies: (1) the formation of the side wall of the braincase from a bone called the anterior lamina, contrasting with the alisphenoid in therian mammals, and (2) a linear alignment of molar cusps, contrasting with the triangular arrangement seen in therians. These features appeared to unite monotremes with a range of Mesozoic fossil orders (Morganucodonta, Triconodonta, Docodonta, and Multituberculata) into a broader clade, for which the name Prototheria was retained. Monotremes were thought to represent the last surviving branch of this clade. However, the evidence supporting this grouping is now universally discounted. Examination of embryonic development has shown that the formation of the braincase wall is essentially identical in therians and prototherians. In therians, the anterior lamina simply fuses with the alisphenoid, indicating that the prototherian condition of the braincase wall is primitive for all mammals, while the therian condition is derived from it. Additionally, the linear alignment of molar cusps is also primitive for all mammals. Therefore, neither of these features can provide a uniquely shared derived character to support a prototherian grouping of orders distinct from Theria. Further reappraisal of embryonic and fossil monotreme molars (since living monotreme adults are toothless) has revealed an ancestral cusp pattern similar to the triangular arrangement observed in therians. Some peculiarities of this dentition support an alternative grouping of monotremes with certain recently discovered fossil forms into a proposed new clade called Australosphenida. This also suggests that the triangular arrangement of cusps may have evolved independently in australosphenidans and therians. Despite these findings, some researchers (e.g., McKenna & Bell, 1997) prefer to retain the name Prototheria as a useful contrast to the other group of living mammals, the Theria. In theory, Prototheria is taxonomically redundant, as Monotremata is currently the only order confidently included within it. However, its retention might be justified if new fossil evidence, or a re-examination of known fossils, allows extinct relatives of monotremes to be identified and placed within a broader grouping.
